questions.title: CTEs (Common Table Expressions) Explained
questions.question: What is a CTE in SQL and when should you prefer it over a subquery?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- CTE: named temporary result set defined with WITH keyword, scoped to one query
- Improves readability by breaking complex queries into named steps
- Recursive CTEs: traverse hierarchical data like org charts or graph edges
- Performance: PostgreSQL treats non-recursive CTEs as optimization fences (materialized by default before 12)
- Difference from subquery: CTEs can be referenced multiple times; subqueries repeat their work
- WITH RECURSIVE: requires anchor query UNION ALL recursive part with termination condition

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A CTE, or Common Table Expression, is a named temporary result set you define at the top of a query using the WITH keyword. It lives only for the duration of that single statement. The main benefit is readability — instead of deeply nested subqueries you break a complex query into clearly named steps that read like paragraphs of a story.

CTEs can also be referenced multiple times within the same query, whereas a subquery gets re-executed each time it's referenced. This matters for both performance and avoiding code duplication.

Recursive CTEs are a uniquely powerful tool for traversing hierarchical data. You define an anchor query that gives you the starting rows, then a recursive part that keeps joining back to the CTE itself to walk down the hierarchy. This is how you find all subordinates of a manager in an org chart, or all descendants of a category in a product tree.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Basic CTE vs Nested Subquery

```sql
-- Hard to read nested subquery
SELECT name FROM (
    SELECT name, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS avg_sal, salary
    FROM employees
) t WHERE salary > avg_sal;

-- Same logic as a readable CTE
WITH dept_averages AS (
    SELECT name, department, salary,
           AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg
    FROM employees
)
SELECT name, department, salary
FROM dept_averages
WHERE salary > dept_avg;
```

## Chaining CTEs

```sql
WITH
recent_orders AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
    FROM orders
    WHERE created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
high_value AS (
    SELECT customer_id, total
    FROM recent_orders
    WHERE total > 1000
)
SELECT c.name, hv.total
FROM high_value hv
JOIN customers c ON hv.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY hv.total DESC;
```

## Recursive CTE — Org Chart

```sql
-- Walk all reports under manager id=1
WITH RECURSIVE org_tree AS (
    -- Anchor: start with the manager
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth
    FROM employees
    WHERE id = 1

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive: join to children, increment depth
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, ot.depth + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN org_tree ot ON e.manager_id = ot.id
)
SELECT id, name, depth FROM org_tree ORDER BY depth, name;
```

## Performance Note

In PostgreSQL 12+, CTEs are inlined by default (same as subqueries). To force materialization:
```sql
WITH cte AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT ... FROM big_table)
SELECT * FROM cte JOIN cte c2 ON ...;
-- Computes once, reuses twice
```

speakable_v2.hook: A CTE, or Common Table Expression, is a named temporary result set you define at the top of a query using the WITH keyword.
speakable_v2.cap: This is how you find all subordinates of a manager in an org chart, or all descendants of a category in a product tree.

questions.title: Types of SQL Subqueries
questions.question: What are the different types of SQL subqueries and when do you use each?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Scalar subquery: returns single value, used in SELECT or WHERE
- Row subquery: returns one row, compared with ROW() constructor
- Table subquery (derived table): in FROM clause, treated like a table
- Correlated subquery: references outer query — re-executes per outer row, can be slow
- EXISTS / NOT EXISTS: often faster than IN for correlated checks — stops at first match
- IN vs EXISTS: IN materializes a list; EXISTS short-circuits at first match

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
There are several kinds of subqueries categorized by where they appear and what they return. A scalar subquery appears in a SELECT clause and returns exactly one value — for example, calculating each employee's salary relative to the company average in a single query without joining. A derived table subquery sits in the FROM clause and behaves like a temporary table, which lets you filter or aggregate before joining to other tables.

Correlated subqueries are the most important to understand for performance. They reference a column from the outer query, which means the database re-executes the inner query for every row the outer query processes. For a million-row outer table, that inner query runs a million times. When you see a correlated subquery in slow code, the fix is usually to rewrite it as a JOIN or a window function.

EXISTS is a semi-join — it checks whether any row exists in a subquery and stops at the first match. It's often faster than IN for correlated conditions because IN builds a full list in memory while EXISTS short-circuits.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Scalar Subquery

```sql
-- Each employee's salary vs company average, in one pass
SELECT name, salary,
       (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees) AS company_avg,
       salary - (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees) AS diff
FROM employees;
-- Better with CTE to compute avg once:
```

## Derived Table (in FROM)

```sql
-- Aggregate first, then join — avoids joining before aggregation
SELECT c.name, d.order_count, d.total
FROM customers c
JOIN (
    SELECT customer_id,
           COUNT(*) AS order_count,
           SUM(amount) AS total
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
) d ON c.id = d.customer_id
WHERE d.order_count > 5;
```

## Correlated Subquery — Watch for Performance

```sql
-- Correlated: re-runs inner query for EVERY employee row
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees e
WHERE salary > (
    SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE department = e.department  -- references outer e
);

-- Rewrite as window function (single pass, much faster)
SELECT name, salary FROM (
    SELECT name, salary, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg
    FROM employees
) t WHERE salary > dept_avg;
```

## EXISTS vs IN

```sql
-- IN: builds list of all matching IDs, then checks membership
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE amount > 500);

-- EXISTS: stops at first match — often faster with large subsets
SELECT name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.amount > 500
);

-- NOT EXISTS (anti-join) — customers with no orders
SELECT name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
);
```

speakable_v2.hook: There are several kinds of subqueries categorized by where they appear and what they return.
speakable_v2.cap: It's often faster than IN for correlated conditions because IN builds a full list in memory while EXISTS short-circuits.

questions.title: UNION vs UNION ALL and Set Operations
questions.question: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL, and what are the other SQL set operations?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- UNION: combines results, removes duplicates — requires extra sort/hash pass
- UNION ALL: combines results, keeps duplicates — faster, preferred when duplicates are impossible or wanted
- INTERSECT: rows appearing in both result sets
- EXCEPT: rows in first result set not in second
- All set operations require same number of columns with compatible types
- Real-world: UNION ALL for combining sharded tables, reports from multiple periods

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
UNION and UNION ALL both stack results from two queries together. The difference is that UNION removes duplicate rows by sorting the combined result and comparing — that extra work costs CPU and time. UNION ALL keeps everything, including duplicates, and is significantly faster.

In practice, prefer UNION ALL unless you specifically need to deduplicate. If you know the two queries return disjoint data — like sales from January and sales from February — there can't be duplicates anyway, so UNION would just be wasted effort.

INTERSECT gives you rows that appear in both result sets, and EXCEPT gives you rows from the first set that don't appear in the second. Both are set-difference operations. In most practical scenarios, joins and anti-joins achieve the same results and often perform better because the optimizer has more flexibility.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## UNION vs UNION ALL

```sql
-- UNION removes duplicates (slower — needs sort/hash)
SELECT email FROM active_users
UNION
SELECT email FROM beta_users;  -- emails appearing in both → deduplicated

-- UNION ALL keeps duplicates (faster)
SELECT product_id, amount, 'Q1' AS quarter FROM q1_sales
UNION ALL
SELECT product_id, amount, 'Q2' AS quarter FROM q2_sales;
-- These quarters can't overlap, so ALL is correct and faster
```

## INTERSECT and EXCEPT

```sql
-- INTERSECT: customers who bought in both Jan AND Feb
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31'
INTERSECT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-02-01' AND '2024-02-28';

-- EXCEPT: customers who bought in Jan but NOT Feb (lapsed customers)
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31'
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-02-01' AND '2024-02-28';
```

## Common Pattern — Full Report

```sql
-- Combine data from multiple tables into a unified view
SELECT id, name, 'employee' AS type FROM employees
UNION ALL
SELECT id, company_name, 'vendor' AS type FROM vendors
UNION ALL
SELECT id, name, 'contractor' AS type FROM contractors
ORDER BY name;
```

speakable_v2.hook: UNION and UNION ALL both stack results from two queries together.
speakable_v2.cap: In most practical scenarios, joins and anti-joins achieve the same results and often perform better because the optimizer has more flexibility.

questions.title: LATERAL Joins and Cross Apply
questions.question: What is a LATERAL join in SQL and what problem does it solve that a regular join cannot?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- LATERAL: allows a subquery in FROM to reference columns from tables to its left
- Regular derived table cannot reference outer tables — it is evaluated independently
- Equivalent to SQL Server's CROSS APPLY
- Common use case: top-N rows per group (more flexible than window function approach)
- Performance: runs per outer row — use when there's no set-based alternative

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A regular derived table in a FROM clause is isolated — it cannot see columns from other tables earlier in the FROM list. A LATERAL join removes that restriction, letting the subquery reference the outer table's current row values. This makes it like a correlated subquery but appearing in the FROM clause so you can return multiple rows or columns.

The most practical use case is getting top-N rows per group in a clean way. You join your main table CROSS JOIN LATERAL a subquery that filters using the outer table's key and applies a LIMIT. This is more flexible than the window function approach when you need to join to other tables within that top-N selection.

Think of it as a loop: for each row on the left side, the LATERAL subquery runs once with that row's values available. This is intentionally per-row execution, so use it when there's no pure set-based alternative.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Regular Derived Table vs LATERAL

```sql
-- FAILS: derived table cannot reference outer tables
SELECT c.name, o.*
FROM customers c
JOIN (
    SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id -- Error! c.id not in scope
    LIMIT 3
) o ON true;

-- WORKS: LATERAL allows c.id reference
SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount, o.created_at
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT id, amount, created_at
    FROM orders
    WHERE customer_id = c.id
    ORDER BY created_at DESC
    LIMIT 3
) o;
-- Returns each customer's 3 most recent orders
```

## Top-N Per Group with LATERAL

```sql
-- 3 highest-revenue products per category
SELECT cat.name AS category, p.title, p.revenue
FROM categories cat
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT title, revenue
    FROM products
    WHERE category_id = cat.id
    ORDER BY revenue DESC
    LIMIT 3
) p
ORDER BY cat.name, p.revenue DESC;
```

## LATERAL with Function

```sql
-- unnest() returns set — LATERAL is implicit for set-returning functions
SELECT u.name, tag
FROM users u
CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(u.tags) AS tag
WHERE tag LIKE '%java%';
```

speakable_v2.hook: A regular derived table in a FROM clause is isolated — it cannot see columns from other tables earlier in the FROM list.
speakable_v2.cap: This is intentionally per-row execution, so use it when there's no pure set-based alternative.

questions.title: Self Joins and Hierarchical Queries
questions.question: What is a self join and what real-world problems does it solve?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Self join: joining a table to itself using two different aliases
- Required when rows in the same table have relationships to each other
- Classic use cases: employee-manager, product-product comparison, friend connections
- Recursive CTE vs self join: self join traverses one level; recursive CTE walks entire hierarchy
- Alias is mandatory to distinguish the two references to the same table

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A self join is when you join a table to itself using two different aliases. It's needed when rows in the same table have relationships with other rows in that same table. The classic example is an employees table where each employee has a manager ID that references another row in the same employees table.

With a self join, you can query both the employee's details and the manager's details in a single row of results — employee name, employee salary, manager name, manager salary — because you're essentially treating the table as two separate tables for the duration of the join.

Self joins traverse only one level of a hierarchy. If you need to walk the full depth — all reports under a manager, all subcategories under a category — you need a recursive CTE instead. Self joins are simpler and more readable when you just need to compare one row against related rows in the same dataset.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Employee-Manager Self Join

```sql
-- Find each employee and their manager's name and salary
SELECT e.name     AS employee,
       e.salary   AS emp_salary,
       m.name     AS manager,
       m.salary   AS mgr_salary
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
-- LEFT JOIN: includes employees with no manager (top of tree)
```

## Finding Discrepancies

```sql
-- Employees earning MORE than their manager
SELECT e.name, e.salary, m.name AS manager, m.salary AS mgr_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
```

## Product Comparison Self Join

```sql
-- Find all product pairs in the same category priced within 10% of each other
SELECT a.title, a.price, b.title AS similar, b.price AS similar_price
FROM products a
JOIN products b ON a.category_id = b.category_id
               AND a.id < b.id  -- avoid (A,B) and (B,A) duplicates
               AND ABS(a.price - b.price) / a.price < 0.1;
```

## One Level vs Full Hierarchy

```sql
-- Self join: direct reports only (one level)
SELECT e.name, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE m.id = 1;

-- Recursive CTE: entire subtree (all levels)
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id FROM employees WHERE id = 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id
    FROM employees e JOIN tree t ON e.manager_id = t.id
)
SELECT * FROM tree;
```

speakable_v2.hook: A self join is when you join a table to itself using two different aliases.
speakable_v2.cap: Self joins are simpler and more readable when you just need to compare one row against related rows in the same dataset.

questions.title: Optimizing Queries with Multiple JOINs
questions.question: What should you keep in mind when writing queries with multiple JOINs for performance and correctness?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Filter early: use WHERE conditions that reduce intermediate result sizes before later joins
- Join order: optimizer usually handles this but you can hint with smaller tables first
- Ensure join columns are indexed — unindexed join = full scan on each join
- Fanout problem: joining to a one-to-many before aggregating inflates counts
- EXPLAIN ANALYZE to spot hash joins, nested loops, seq scans indicating missing indexes
- Use derived tables / CTEs to pre-aggregate before joining to avoid inflated row counts

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The biggest correctness issue with multiple joins is the fanout problem. If you join orders to order_items before aggregating, each order row multiplies by the number of items. Summing order amounts in that state gives you wrong numbers because every amount appears once per item. The fix is to aggregate order_items into a derived table first, then join the summary to orders.

For performance, make sure every join column is indexed. When you join on customer_id, the database needs to look up matching rows for every value it encounters. Without an index on that foreign key column, each lookup scans the entire table. EXPLAIN ANALYZE will show you nested loop scans with high row estimates as a red flag.

Filter as early as possible. A WHERE condition on the first table in the FROM clause reduces the size of every subsequent intermediate result. Pushing filters into derived tables or CTEs explicitly gives the optimizer more information to work with.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Fanout Problem — Inflated Aggregates

```sql
-- WRONG: joins line items before summing → each order's total multiplied per item
SELECT o.id, c.name, SUM(o.total_amount) AS wrong_total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id  -- inflates rows!
GROUP BY o.id, c.name;

-- RIGHT: aggregate order_items first, then join
SELECT o.id, c.name, oi_summary.item_count, o.total_amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN (
    SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS item_count
    FROM order_items
    GROUP BY order_id
) oi_summary ON oi_summary.order_id = o.id;
```

## Index Your Join Columns

```sql
-- For this query:
SELECT o.*, c.name, p.title
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN products  p ON o.product_id  = p.id;

-- Ensure these indexes exist:
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (product_id);
-- customers.id and products.id already indexed as PKs
```

## Reading EXPLAIN Output

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT ... FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON ...;

-- Good signs: Index Scan, low actual rows
-- Warning signs: Seq Scan on large table, Hash Join with large batch
-- Nested Loop with large outer rows = missing index on inner table
```

## Pre-filter in CTEs for Readability and Performance

```sql
WITH recent_orders AS (
    SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
),
high_value_customers AS (
    SELECT customer_id FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) > 5000
)
SELECT c.name, ro.id, ro.amount
FROM recent_orders ro
JOIN customers c ON ro.customer_id = c.id
JOIN high_value_customers hvc ON ro.customer_id = hvc.customer_id;
```

speakable_v2.hook: The biggest correctness issue with multiple joins is the fanout problem.
speakable_v2.cap: Pushing filters into derived tables or CTEs explicitly gives the optimizer more information to work with.

questions.title: EXISTS vs IN vs JOIN for Filtering
questions.question: When should you use EXISTS, IN, or JOIN when filtering rows based on a related table?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- JOIN: use when you need columns from the related table; may inflate rows (one-to-many)
- IN: good for simple value-list lookups; can degrade with very large subquery results
- EXISTS: semi-join — short-circuits at first match; no row inflation; best for existence checks
- NOT IN with NULLs is a trap — if subquery contains any NULL, result is always empty
- NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe and generally preferred over NOT IN
- Modern optimizers often rewrite IN to EXISTS anyway, but knowing the semantics matters

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Use JOIN when you need actual column values from the related table. Use EXISTS or IN when you only need to check whether a relationship exists — you don't need any columns from the related table.

EXISTS is a semi-join — the database checks for the existence of at least one matching row and stops immediately when it finds one. This makes it efficient and avoids inflating the result set when there are multiple matching rows in the related table. JOIN would duplicate the outer row for each match.

The critical trap with NOT IN is NULLs. If your subquery returns even one NULL value, NOT IN returns no rows at all because SQL cannot determine that the outer value is definitely not equal to an unknown value. NOT EXISTS does not have this problem — it's always safe to use for anti-join patterns.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Choosing the Right Approach

```sql
-- JOIN: need columns from orders too
SELECT c.name, o.amount, o.created_at
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'completed';
-- If customer has 5 orders, customer appears 5 times

-- EXISTS: just checking if customer HAS an order
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'completed'
);
-- Each customer appears once; stops at first match

-- IN: equivalent for simple cases
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed');
```

## The NOT IN NULL Trap

```sql
-- Suppose orders has one row with customer_id = NULL
-- This returns ZERO rows — completely wrong!
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders); -- NULL makes NOT IN useless

-- Safe alternative: NOT EXISTS
SELECT name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
);

-- Or filter NULLs explicitly
WHERE id NOT IN (
    SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
);
```

## Performance Summary

| Approach | Row Inflation | NULL-safe | Use When |
|----------|--------------|-----------|----------|
| JOIN | Yes (one-to-many) | N/A | Need related columns |
| IN | No | NOT IN unsafe | Simple list check |
| EXISTS | No | Yes | Existence check, anti-join |

speakable_v2.hook: Use JOIN when you need actual column values from the related table.
speakable_v2.cap: NOT EXISTS does not have this problem — it's always safe to use for anti-join patterns.
